title: Pivot 1 — Where Did Submit Go? (GET vs POST)
description: How a submitted form travels through CodeIgniter 3: controllers, URL segments, GET vs POST, and what a 404 actually proves.
congratsText: You mastered Pivot 1 — GET vs POST!
objectives: Identify the form attribute that decides where submitted data is sent
Explain which jobs belong to the client and which belong to the server
Write a controller class CI3 will recognize and run
Read a CI3 URL and name its controller and method segments
Compare GET and POST by where the submitted data travels
Choose the safe method for a form that carries a password
Explain what a CI3 404 error proves about the request
Apply $this->input->post() to read submitted fields inside a controller
recap: The action attribute names the destination a submitted form travels to.
The browser can only display; the server is the side that runs PHP and saves data.
A CI3 controller is a PHP class that extends CI_Controller, saved in application/controllers/.
A URL's first segment names the controller class, the second names the method.
GET attaches the fields to the URL; POST carries them inside the request body.
Passwords go by POST, because a GET URL is visible on screen and in browser history.
A 404 proves CI3 received the request and found no matching controller or method.
$this->input->post() reads submitted fields, keyed by each input's name attribute.

sections.title: Click Submit — Where Does It Go?

chunks.text: You fill out a form and click Submit. The browser packs up what you typed and sends it somewhere.

check.question: Who packs up the typed values on Submit?

chunks.text: That "somewhere" is set by the form's action attribute — point it at a destination that isn't ready, and the trip goes nowhere.
A plain HTML page cannot read what you typed. Something sitting on the server has to catch the data.

check.question: Can a plain HTML page read submitted data?

quiz.question: In this form tag, which attribute decides where the submitted data travels?
options: method — it sets how data is sent to the server
name — it labels each individual input
id — it identifies the form in the page

sections.title: Client vs Server — Two Computers, Two Jobs

chunks.text: Two computers are always involved. The client is the browser on your screen.
The server is the computer that stores the site's files and runs its code.
Think of a restaurant: you place the order, the kitchen cooks it. A browser can show a page, but it cannot check a password.

chunks.text: Set a form's method to get, and the browser tacks every field onto the end of the web address.

sections.title: Seeing GET's Danger — A Password in Plain Sight

chunks.text: Take the login form from the earlier lab, switch one attribute to GET, and submit it.
The password now sits in the address bar for anyone nearby to read, and it gets saved into the browser's history.

check.question: Where is the password now visible?

chunks.text: This is why GET is never used for passwords, or for anything that should stay private — framework or no framework.

check.question: Is GET ever acceptable for a password?

sections.title: CI3's 404 — Proof the Controller Wasn't There

chunks.text: Point a form's action at a method that doesn't exist yet, like pivot/store, and submit it.
CI3 answers with its own 404 error page — and that error is good news.
A 404 means "I looked, and found nothing to run." The trip worked; the destination just isn't built yet.

quiz.question: This form is submitted and CI3 answers with a 404. Which part of the tag points at the missing destination?
options: The method value — it names how to send
The action value — it names where to send
The form tag itself — it blocks submission
The submit button — it picks the controller

Both mistakes end on the same 404 page — one is a missing method, the other a missing class.
